Date: Tue, 16 Aug 2022 15:46:37 -0600
From: Shaun Cooney <shaun@monumentgraphics.com>
To:   eric@ericphiferllc.com
Subject: Meeting Follow-up

Hi Eric,

Great meeting you today!

The Aspen site I was referencing today is aspenrecreation.com. The current dev team has set up their dev environment using Docker. From what I can see, it looks like a combination of PostCSS, Tailwind & Vue. I think there might be some GraphQL in there as well, but I’m not 100% sure. It’s built using Craft CMS (uses twig) and is hosted with a company called Servd. The calendar is located here: https://www.aspenrecreation.com/sports-activities/calendar and pipes in data from all the activity pages. I was primarily responsible for designing the site (though like your story, the design deviates significantly from the XD files), but had almost nothing to do with the coding, so most of it is rather foreign to me.

A few examples of sites I’ve handled top to bottom are:
Wiggys.com - BigCommerce store. Doesn’t look like much, but the guy does well over $1M in online sales per year.
BuffaloCollection.com - Another BigCommerce store
BuffaloBoutique.com - Squarespace site serving as a temporary landing page for a spin-off store to Buffalo Collection that I’m currently developing in BigCommerce.
Climb13ers.com - the other Craft site (belongs to my dad; I’ve taken on a more active role in maintaining this one)
COFAWellness.com - Squarespace site
RedBrickAspen.com - Older Squarespace site

Overall, web is probably about 40-50% of what I do. The rest is mostly graphic design-oriented with a little SEO and other marketing scattered in there along with more IT support than I care to admit :)

If you’d be interested in learning more about the Aspen site let me know and I’ll see if I can clear access with the Aspen team. Feel free to reach out with any questions and I look forward to keeping in touch!

Shaun Cooney } MONUMENT GRAPHICS | DESIGN + WEB
PO Box 299, Fruita, CO 81521
p* 970/242-4311 • MonumentGraphics.com

> > > > > > > > > > > On Nov 10, 2025 at 12:59 PM -0700, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>, wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > >  Hi Shaun,
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting together:
> > > > > > > > > > > > There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for each.
> > > > > > > > > > > > A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
> > > > > > > > > > > > Where to edit: Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Why: Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> > > > > > > > > > > > Simple steps
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > In Production, open the entry → Create Draft → review (use Preview) → Publish when approved.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior Revision at any time. Craft CMS: Entries
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > When not to do this: If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Rollback (content): Restore the previous Revision of the entry, or restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
> > > > > > > > > > > > Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Steps
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > Staging → set its bundle to match Production (code parity). Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
> > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > Clone Production → Staging (DB + assets). This overwrites Staging; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
> > > > > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > > > > Make/review content changes on Staging.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > > > > Clone Staging → Production (DB + assets) to launch.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Timing: Do this in a short window off-hours. The clone replaces Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm. (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
> > > > > > > > > > > > Rollback (content via clone): Restore Production from Servd backup or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> > > > > > > > > > > > B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — no schema
> > > > > > > > > > > > Policy: Production does not auto-build from merges. We promote the tested Staging bundle to Production.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > Open a PR into staging; merge when approved.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > Servd builds a new bundle for Staging from that commit; test the site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
> > > > > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > > > > In Servd → Production → assign the same Staging bundle (Deploy/Assign Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > > > > Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Rollback (code): In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous known-good bundle.
> > > > > > > > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > > > > > > > # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> > > > > > > > > > > > # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
> > > > > > > > > > > > Then test Staging and assign the Staging bundle to Production in Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> > > > > > > > > > > > C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
> > > > > > > > > > > > These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.). They must move via Project Config and migrations.
> > > > > > > > > > > > Important defaults: In Production, allowAdminChanges should be false so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
> > > > > > > > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > Make the settings/field changes on Staging CMS (or local with admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > Commit & merge to staging; Servd builds a bundle.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > > > > Staging deploy runs your Post-Deploy Tasks: craft up (migrations + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
> > > > > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > > > > In Servd, assign the same bundle to Production. The same Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Rollback (schema):
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > > > > Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous bundle.
> > > > > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > > > > If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the Production DB backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > > > > > > > # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)
> > > > > > > > > > > > # Commit project config & composer updates
> > > > > > > > > > > > git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> > > > > > > > > > > > git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> > > > > > > > > > > > git push origin staging
> > > > > > > > > > > > # Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
> > > > > > > > > > > > On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually (rare):
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > > > > php craft up --interactive=0
> > > > > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > > > > php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > When Staging passes QA, assign the same bundle to Production (Servd UI).
> > > > > > > > > > > > D) Assets (practical note)
> > > > > > > > > > > > Use the Servd Asset Platform + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s clone/import between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets

Since the heading button text use a plain text field, I assume the current method isn’t an option. Potential solutions I can think of are:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > What are your thoughts on this? I’m looking for the best solution that satisfies the WCAG 2.2 AA spec, doesn’t muddy the editing process, while also not creating a ton of work.

>>>> On Nov 10, 2025 at 12:59 PM -0700, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>,
>>>> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>  Hi Shaun,
>>>>
>>>> Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.
>>>>
>>>> The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting
>>>> together:
>>>>
>>>> There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different
>>>> for each.
>>>> A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
>>>>
>>>> *Where to edit:* Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when
>>>> ready.
>>>> *Why:* Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content
>>>> edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS:
>>>> Revisions
>>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/drafts-revisions.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> *Simple steps*
>>>>
>>>>    1.
>>>>
>>>>    In Production, open the entry → *Create Draft* → review (use
>>>>    Preview) → *Publish* when approved.
>>>>    2.
>>>>
>>>>    If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior *Revision* at any
>>>>    time. Craft CMS: Entries
>>>>    <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/reference/element-types/entries.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>
>>>> *When not to do this:* If Production content is corrupted or must
>>>> rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow
>>>> below.
>>>>
>>>> *Rollback (content):* Restore the previous *Revision* of the entry, or
>>>> restore a Production DB backup if needed.
>>>> ------------------------------
>>>> Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
>>>>
>>>> Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match
>>>> Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back
>>>> to Production.
>>>>
>>>> *Steps*
>>>>
>>>>    1.
>>>>
>>>>    Staging → set its *bundle* to match Production (code parity).
>>>>    Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host:
>>>>    Bundles
>>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/whats-a-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>    2.
>>>>
>>>>    *Clone Production → Staging* (DB + assets). This *overwrites
>>>>    Staging*; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an
>>>>    Environment
>>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/cloning-an-environment?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>    3.
>>>>
>>>>    Make/review content changes on Staging.
>>>>    4.
>>>>
>>>>    *Clone Staging → Production* (DB + assets) to launch.
>>>>
>>>> *Timing:* Do this in a short window *off-hours*. The clone replaces
>>>> Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm.
>>>> (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
>>>>
>>>> *Rollback (content via clone):* Restore Production from Servd backup
>>>> or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting &
>>>> Deployment
>>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/deploy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>> ------------------------------
>>>> B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — *no schema*
>>>>
>>>> *Policy:* Production does *not* auto-build from merges. We promote the *tested
>>>> Staging bundle* to Production.
>>>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>>>
>>>>    1.
>>>>
>>>>    Open a PR into *staging*; merge when approved.
>>>>    2.
>>>>
>>>>    Servd builds a new *bundle* for Staging from that commit; test the
>>>>    site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
>>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/create-a-new-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>    3.
>>>>
>>>>    In Servd → *Production* → assign *the same Staging bundle* (Deploy/Assign
>>>>    Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
>>>>    4.
>>>>
>>>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will
>>>>    no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
>>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/post-deploy-tasks?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>
>>>> *Rollback (code):* In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous
>>>> known-good bundle.
>>>> CLI path (for devs)
>>>>
>>>> # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
>>>> # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push
>>>> origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging
>>>> git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
>>>>
>>>> Then test Staging and *assign the Staging bundle to Production* in
>>>> Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
>>>> ------------------------------
>>>> C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
>>>>
>>>> These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings,
>>>> etc.). They must move via *Project Config* and migrations.
>>>>
>>>> *Important defaults:* In Production, allowAdminChanges should be
>>>> *false* so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and
>>>> deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
>>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/project-config.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>>>
>>>>    1.
>>>>
>>>>    Make the settings/field changes on *Staging CMS* (or local with
>>>>    admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
>>>>    2.
>>>>
>>>>    Commit & merge to *staging*; Servd builds a bundle.
>>>>    3.
>>>>
>>>>    Staging deploy runs your *Post-Deploy Tasks*: craft up (migrations
>>>>    + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging
>>>>    works.
>>>>    4.
>>>>
>>>>    In Servd, *assign the same bundle* to *Production*. The same
>>>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
>>>>
>>>> *Rollback (schema):*
>>>>
>>>>    -
>>>>
>>>>    Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous
>>>>    bundle.
>>>>    -
>>>>
>>>>    If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the *Production
>>>>    DB* backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
>>>>
>>>> CLI path (for devs)
>>>>
>>>> # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)# Commit project config & composer updates
>>>> git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
>>>> git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
>>>> git push origin staging# Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
>>>>
>>>> On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually
>>>> (rare):
>>>>
>>>>    -
>>>>
>>>>    php craft up --interactive=0
>>>>    -
>>>>
>>>>    php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
>>>>    <https://craftcms.stackexchange.com/questions/41038/run-craft-up-command-in-deployment-pipeline-without-prompts?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>
>>>> When Staging passes QA, *assign the same bundle to Production* (Servd
>>>> UI).
>>>> ------------------------------
>>>> D) Assets (practical note)
>>>>
>>>> Use the *Servd Asset Platform* + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and
>>>> Servd’s *clone/import* between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to
>>>> Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host:
>>>> Assets <https://servd.host/docs/assets?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>>

> > > > > > > > > The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting together:
> > > > > > > > > There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for each.
> > > > > > > > > A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
> > > > > > > > > Where to edit: Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
> > > > > > > > > Why: Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> > > > > > > > > Simple steps
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > In Production, open the entry → Create Draft → review (use Preview) → Publish when approved.
> > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior Revision at any time. Craft CMS: Entries
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > When not to do this: If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.
> > > > > > > > > Rollback (content): Restore the previous Revision of the entry, or restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> > > > > > > > > Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
> > > > > > > > > Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
> > > > > > > > > Steps
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > Staging → set its bundle to match Production (code parity). Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
> > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > Clone Production → Staging (DB + assets). This overwrites Staging; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
> > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > Make/review content changes on Staging.
> > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > Clone Staging → Production (DB + assets) to launch.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Timing: Do this in a short window off-hours. The clone replaces Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm. (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
> > > > > > > > > Rollback (content via clone): Restore Production from Servd backup or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> > > > > > > > > B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — no schema
> > > > > > > > > Policy: Production does not auto-build from merges. We promote the tested Staging bundle to Production.
> > > > > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > Open a PR into staging; merge when approved.
> > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > Servd builds a new bundle for Staging from that commit; test the site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
> > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > In Servd → Production → assign the same Staging bundle (Deploy/Assign Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
> > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Rollback (code): In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous known-good bundle.
> > > > > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > > > > # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> > > > > > > > > # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
> > > > > > > > > Then test Staging and assign the Staging bundle to Production in Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> > > > > > > > > C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
> > > > > > > > > These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.). They must move via Project Config and migrations.
> > > > > > > > > Important defaults: In Production, allowAdminChanges should be false so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
> > > > > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > Make the settings/field changes on Staging CMS (or local with admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
> > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > Commit & merge to staging; Servd builds a bundle.
> > > > > > > > > 3. > > > > > > > > > Staging deploy runs your Post-Deploy Tasks: craft up (migrations + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
> > > > > > > > > 4. > > > > > > > > > In Servd, assign the same bundle to Production. The same Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Rollback (schema):
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous bundle.
> > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the Production DB backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > > > > # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)
> > > > > > > > > # Commit project config & composer updates
> > > > > > > > > git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> > > > > > > > > git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> > > > > > > > > git push origin staging
> > > > > > > > > # Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
> > > > > > > > > On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually (rare):
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > php craft up --interactive=0
> > > > > > > > > • > > > > > > > > > php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > When Staging passes QA, assign the same bundle to Production (Servd UI).
> > > > > > > > > D) Assets (practical note)
> > > > > > > > > Use the Servd Asset Platform + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s clone/import between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

>>> On Nov 10, 2025 at 12:59 PM -0700, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>,
>>> wrote:
>>>
>>>  Hi Shaun,
>>>
>>> Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.
>>>
>>> The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting
>>> together:
>>>
>>> There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for
>>> each.
>>> A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
>>>
>>> *Where to edit:* Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when
>>> ready.
>>> *Why:* Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content
>>> edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS:
>>> Revisions
>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/drafts-revisions.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>
>>>
>>> *Simple steps*
>>>
>>>    1.
>>>
>>>    In Production, open the entry → *Create Draft* → review (use
>>>    Preview) → *Publish* when approved.
>>>    2.
>>>
>>>    If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior *Revision* at any
>>>    time. Craft CMS: Entries
>>>    <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/reference/element-types/entries.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>
>>> *When not to do this:* If Production content is corrupted or must
>>> rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow
>>> below.
>>>
>>> *Rollback (content):* Restore the previous *Revision* of the entry, or
>>> restore a Production DB backup if needed.
>>> ------------------------------
>>> Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
>>>
>>> Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production,
>>> practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
>>>
>>> *Steps*
>>>
>>>    1.
>>>
>>>    Staging → set its *bundle* to match Production (code parity).
>>>    Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host:
>>>    Bundles
>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/whats-a-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>    2.
>>>
>>>    *Clone Production → Staging* (DB + assets). This *overwrites Staging*;
>>>    make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/cloning-an-environment?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>    3.
>>>
>>>    Make/review content changes on Staging.
>>>    4.
>>>
>>>    *Clone Staging → Production* (DB + assets) to launch.
>>>
>>> *Timing:* Do this in a short window *off-hours*. The clone replaces
>>> Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm.
>>> (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
>>>
>>> *Rollback (content via clone):* Restore Production from Servd backup or
>>> re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/deploy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>> ------------------------------
>>> B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — *no schema*
>>>
>>> *Policy:* Production does *not* auto-build from merges. We promote the *tested
>>> Staging bundle* to Production.
>>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>>
>>>    1.
>>>
>>>    Open a PR into *staging*; merge when approved.
>>>    2.
>>>
>>>    Servd builds a new *bundle* for Staging from that commit; test the
>>>    site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/create-a-new-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>    3.
>>>
>>>    In Servd → *Production* → assign *the same Staging bundle* (Deploy/Assign
>>>    Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
>>>    4.
>>>
>>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will
>>>    no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
>>>    <https://servd.host/docs/post-deploy-tasks?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>
>>> *Rollback (code):* In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous
>>> known-good bundle.
>>> CLI path (for devs)
>>>
>>> # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
>>> # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push
>>> origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging
>>> git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
>>>
>>> Then test Staging and *assign the Staging bundle to Production* in
>>> Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
>>> ------------------------------
>>> C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
>>>
>>> These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings,
>>> etc.). They must move via *Project Config* and migrations.
>>>
>>> *Important defaults:* In Production, allowAdminChanges should be *false* so
>>> schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft
>>> CMS: Project Config
>>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/project-config.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>>
>>>    1.
>>>
>>>    Make the settings/field changes on *Staging CMS* (or local with
>>>    admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
>>>    2.
>>>
>>>    Commit & merge to *staging*; Servd builds a bundle.
>>>    3.
>>>
>>>    Staging deploy runs your *Post-Deploy Tasks*: craft up (migrations +
>>>    project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging
>>>    works.
>>>    4.
>>>
>>>    In Servd, *assign the same bundle* to *Production*. The same
>>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
>>>
>>> *Rollback (schema):*
>>>
>>>    -
>>>
>>>    Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous
>>>    bundle.
>>>    -
>>>
>>>    If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the *Production
>>>    DB* backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
>>>
>>> CLI path (for devs)
>>>
>>> # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)# Commit project config & composer updates
>>> git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
>>> git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
>>> git push origin staging# Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
>>>
>>> On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually
>>> (rare):
>>>
>>>    -
>>>
>>>    php craft up --interactive=0
>>>    -
>>>
>>>    php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
>>>    <https://craftcms.stackexchange.com/questions/41038/run-craft-up-command-in-deployment-pipeline-without-prompts?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>
>>> When Staging passes QA, *assign the same bundle to Production* (Servd
>>> UI).
>>> ------------------------------
>>> D) Assets (practical note)
>>>
>>> Use the *Servd Asset Platform* + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and
>>> Servd’s *clone/import* between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to
>>> Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
>>> <https://servd.host/docs/assets?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>>

> > > > > > The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting together:
> > > > > > There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for each.
> > > > > > A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
> > > > > > Where to edit: Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
> > > > > > Why: Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> > > > > > Simple steps
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 1. > > > > > > In Production, open the entry → Create Draft → review (use Preview) → Publish when approved.
> > > > > > 2. > > > > > > If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior Revision at any time. Craft CMS: Entries
> > > > > >
> > > > > > When not to do this: If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.
> > > > > > Rollback (content): Restore the previous Revision of the entry, or restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> > > > > > Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
> > > > > > Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
> > > > > > Steps
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 1. > > > > > > Staging → set its bundle to match Production (code parity). Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
> > > > > > 2. > > > > > > Clone Production → Staging (DB + assets). This overwrites Staging; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
> > > > > > 3. > > > > > > Make/review content changes on Staging.
> > > > > > 4. > > > > > > Clone Staging → Production (DB + assets) to launch.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Timing: Do this in a short window off-hours. The clone replaces Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm. (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
> > > > > > Rollback (content via clone): Restore Production from Servd backup or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> > > > > > B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — no schema
> > > > > > Policy: Production does not auto-build from merges. We promote the tested Staging bundle to Production.
> > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 1. > > > > > > Open a PR into staging; merge when approved.
> > > > > > 2. > > > > > > Servd builds a new bundle for Staging from that commit; test the site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
> > > > > > 3. > > > > > > In Servd → Production → assign the same Staging bundle (Deploy/Assign Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
> > > > > > 4. > > > > > > Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Rollback (code): In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous known-good bundle.
> > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> > > > > > # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
> > > > > > Then test Staging and assign the Staging bundle to Production in Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> > > > > > C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
> > > > > > These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.). They must move via Project Config and migrations.
> > > > > > Important defaults: In Production, allowAdminChanges should be false so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
> > > > > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 1. > > > > > > Make the settings/field changes on Staging CMS (or local with admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
> > > > > > 2. > > > > > > Commit & merge to staging; Servd builds a bundle.
> > > > > > 3. > > > > > > Staging deploy runs your Post-Deploy Tasks: craft up (migrations + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
> > > > > > 4. > > > > > > In Servd, assign the same bundle to Production. The same Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Rollback (schema):
> > > > > >
> > > > > > • > > > > > > Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous bundle.
> > > > > > • > > > > > > If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the Production DB backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > > > > # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)
> > > > > > # Commit project config & composer updates
> > > > > > git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> > > > > > git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> > > > > > git push origin staging
> > > > > > # Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
> > > > > > On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually (rare):
> > > > > >
> > > > > > • > > > > > > php craft up --interactive=0
> > > > > > • > > > > > > php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
> > > > > >
> > > > > > When Staging passes QA, assign the same bundle to Production (Servd UI).
> > > > > > D) Assets (practical note)
> > > > > > Use the Servd Asset Platform + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s clone/import between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
> > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

>> wrote:
>>
>>  Hi Shaun,

>> Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.

>> The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting
>> together:
>>
>> There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for
>> each.
>> A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
>>
>> *Where to edit:* Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when
>> ready.
>> *Why:* Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content
>> edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/drafts-revisions.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>
>>
>> *Simple steps*
>>
>>    1.
>>
>>    In Production, open the entry → *Create Draft* → review (use Preview)
>>    → *Publish* when approved.
>>    2.
>>
>>    If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior *Revision* at any
>>    time. Craft CMS: Entries
>>    <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/reference/element-types/entries.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>
>> *When not to do this:* If Production content is corrupted or must
>> rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow
>> below.
>>
>> *Rollback (content):* Restore the previous *Revision* of the entry, or
>> restore a Production DB backup if needed.
>> ------------------------------
>> Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
>>
>> Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production,
>> practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
>>
>> *Steps*
>>
>>    1.
>>
>>    Staging → set its *bundle* to match Production (code parity). Bundles
>>    are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
>>    <https://servd.host/docs/whats-a-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>    2.
>>
>>    *Clone Production → Staging* (DB + assets). This *overwrites Staging*;
>>    make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
>>    <https://servd.host/docs/cloning-an-environment?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>    3.
>>
>>    Make/review content changes on Staging.
>>    4.
>>
>>    *Clone Staging → Production* (DB + assets) to launch.
>>
>> *Timing:* Do this in a short window *off-hours*. The clone replaces
>> Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm.
>> (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
>>
>> *Rollback (content via clone):* Restore Production from Servd backup or
>> re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/deploy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>> ------------------------------
>> B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — *no schema*
>>
>> *Policy:* Production does *not* auto-build from merges. We promote the *tested
>> Staging bundle* to Production.
>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>
>>    1.
>>
>>    Open a PR into *staging*; merge when approved.
>>    2.
>>
>>    Servd builds a new *bundle* for Staging from that commit; test the
>>    site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
>>    <https://servd.host/docs/create-a-new-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>    3.
>>
>>    In Servd → *Production* → assign *the same Staging bundle* (Deploy/Assign
>>    Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
>>    4.
>>
>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op;
>>    caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
>>    <https://servd.host/docs/post-deploy-tasks?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>
>> *Rollback (code):* In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous
>> known-good bundle.
>> CLI path (for devs)
>>
>> # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
>> # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin
>> feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull
>> git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
>>
>> Then test Staging and *assign the Staging bundle to Production* in
>> Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
>> ------------------------------
>> C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
>>
>> These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings,
>> etc.). They must move via *Project Config* and migrations.
>>
>> *Important defaults:* In Production, allowAdminChanges should be *false* so
>> schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft
>> CMS: Project Config
>> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/project-config.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>>
>>    1.
>>
>>    Make the settings/field changes on *Staging CMS* (or local with admin
>>    changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
>>    2.
>>
>>    Commit & merge to *staging*; Servd builds a bundle.
>>    3.
>>
>>    Staging deploy runs your *Post-Deploy Tasks*: craft up (migrations +
>>    project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging
>>    works.
>>    4.
>>
>>    In Servd, *assign the same bundle* to *Production*. The same
>>    Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
>>
>> *Rollback (schema):*
>>
>>    -
>>
>>    Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous
>>    bundle.
>>    -
>>
>>    If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the *Production
>>    DB* backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
>>
>> CLI path (for devs)
>>
>> # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)# Commit project config & composer updates
>> git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
>> git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
>> git push origin staging# Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
>>
>> On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually
>> (rare):
>>
>>    -
>>
>>    php craft up --interactive=0
>>    -
>>
>>    php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
>>    <https://craftcms.stackexchange.com/questions/41038/run-craft-up-command-in-deployment-pipeline-without-prompts?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>
>> When Staging passes QA, *assign the same bundle to Production* (Servd
>> UI).
>> ------------------------------
>> D) Assets (practical note)
>>
>> Use the *Servd Asset Platform* + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and
>> Servd’s *clone/import* between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to
>> Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
>> <https://servd.host/docs/assets?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>>

> > >
> > > The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting together:
> > > There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for each.
> > > A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
> > > Where to edit: Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
> > > Why: Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> > > Simple steps
> > >
> > > 1. > > > In Production, open the entry → Create Draft → review (use Preview) → Publish when approved.
> > > 2. > > > If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior Revision at any time. Craft CMS: Entries
> > >
> > > When not to do this: If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.
> > > Rollback (content): Restore the previous Revision of the entry, or restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> > > Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
> > > Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
> > > Steps
> > >
> > > 1. > > > Staging → set its bundle to match Production (code parity). Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
> > > 2. > > > Clone Production → Staging (DB + assets). This overwrites Staging; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
> > > 3. > > > Make/review content changes on Staging.
> > > 4. > > > Clone Staging → Production (DB + assets) to launch.
> > >
> > > Timing: Do this in a short window off-hours. The clone replaces Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm. (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
> > > Rollback (content via clone): Restore Production from Servd backup or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> > > B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — no schema
> > > Policy: Production does not auto-build from merges. We promote the tested Staging bundle to Production.
> > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > >
> > > 1. > > > Open a PR into staging; merge when approved.
> > > 2. > > > Servd builds a new bundle for Staging from that commit; test the site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
> > > 3. > > > In Servd → Production → assign the same Staging bundle (Deploy/Assign Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
> > > 4. > > > Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
> > >
> > > Rollback (code): In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous known-good bundle.
> > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> > > # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
> > > Then test Staging and assign the Staging bundle to Production in Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> > > C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
> > > These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.). They must move via Project Config and migrations.
> > > Important defaults: In Production, allowAdminChanges should be false so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
> > > Click-only path (GitHub App users)
> > >
> > > 1. > > > Make the settings/field changes on Staging CMS (or local with admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
> > > 2. > > > Commit & merge to staging; Servd builds a bundle.
> > > 3. > > > Staging deploy runs your Post-Deploy Tasks: craft up (migrations + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
> > > 4. > > > In Servd, assign the same bundle to Production. The same Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
> > >
> > > Rollback (schema):
> > >
> > > • > > > Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous bundle.
> > > • > > > If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the Production DB backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
> > >
> > > CLI path (for devs)
> > > # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)
> > > # Commit project config & composer updates
> > > git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> > > git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> > > git push origin staging
> > > # Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
> > > On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually (rare):
> > >
> > > • > > > php craft up --interactive=0
> > > • > > > php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
> > >
> > > When Staging passes QA, assign the same bundle to Production (Servd UI).
> > > D) Assets (practical note)
> > > Use the Servd Asset Platform + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s clone/import between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > AR-68: I think we might have (unfortunately) opened up a can of worms on this one. If you look at the scholarships page, there are also two sidebar items that are in Spanish. Since the heading button text use a plain text field, I assume the current method isn’t an option. Potential solutions I can think of are:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

> On Nov 10, 2025 at 12:59 PM -0700, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>,
> wrote:
>
>  Hi Shaun,
>
> Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.
>
> The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting
> together:
>
> There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for
> each.
> A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
>
> *Where to edit:* Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when
> ready.
> *Why:* Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content
> edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/drafts-revisions.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>
>
> *Simple steps*
>
>    1.
>
>    In Production, open the entry → *Create Draft* → review (use Preview) →
>     *Publish* when approved.
>    2.
>
>    If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior *Revision* at any
>    time. Craft CMS: Entries
>    <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/reference/element-types/entries.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>
> *When not to do this:* If Production content is corrupted or must
> rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow
> below.
>
> *Rollback (content):* Restore the previous *Revision* of the entry, or
> restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> ------------------------------
> Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
>
> Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production,
> practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
>
> *Steps*
>
>    1.
>
>    Staging → set its *bundle* to match Production (code parity). Bundles
>    are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
>    <https://servd.host/docs/whats-a-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>    2.
>
>    *Clone Production → Staging* (DB + assets). This *overwrites Staging*;
>    make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
>    <https://servd.host/docs/cloning-an-environment?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>    3.
>
>    Make/review content changes on Staging.
>    4.
>
>    *Clone Staging → Production* (DB + assets) to launch.
>
> *Timing:* Do this in a short window *off-hours*. The clone replaces
> Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm.
> (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
>
> *Rollback (content via clone):* Restore Production from Servd backup or
> re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/deploy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
> ------------------------------
> B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — *no schema*
>
> *Policy:* Production does *not* auto-build from merges. We promote the *tested
> Staging bundle* to Production.
> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>
>    1.
>
>    Open a PR into *staging*; merge when approved.
>    2.
>
>    Servd builds a new *bundle* for Staging from that commit; test the
>    site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
>    <https://servd.host/docs/create-a-new-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>    3.
>
>    In Servd → *Production* → assign *the same Staging bundle* (Deploy/Assign
>    Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
>    4.
>
>    Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op;
>    caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
>    <https://servd.host/docs/post-deploy-tasks?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>
> *Rollback (code):* In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous
> known-good bundle.
> CLI path (for devs)
>
> # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin
> feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull
> git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
>
> Then test Staging and *assign the Staging bundle to Production* in Servd.
> (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> ------------------------------
> C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
>
> These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings,
> etc.). They must move via *Project Config* and migrations.
>
> *Important defaults:* In Production, allowAdminChanges should be *false* so
> schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft
> CMS: Project Config
> <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/project-config.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>
>    1.
>
>    Make the settings/field changes on *Staging CMS* (or local with admin
>    changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
>    2.
>
>    Commit & merge to *staging*; Servd builds a bundle.
>    3.
>
>    Staging deploy runs your *Post-Deploy Tasks*: craft up (migrations +
>    project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging
>    works.
>    4.
>
>    In Servd, *assign the same bundle* to *Production*. The same
>    Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
>
> *Rollback (schema):*
>
>    -
>
>    Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous
>    bundle.
>    -
>
>    If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the *Production
>    DB* backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
>
> CLI path (for devs)
>
> # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)# Commit project config & composer updates
> git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> git push origin staging# Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
>
> On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually
> (rare):
>
>    -
>
>    php craft up --interactive=0
>    -
>
>    php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
>    <https://craftcms.stackexchange.com/questions/41038/run-craft-up-command-in-deployment-pipeline-without-prompts?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>
> When Staging passes QA, *assign the same bundle to Production* (Servd UI).
> ------------------------------
> D) Assets (practical note)
>
> Use the *Servd Asset Platform* + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and
> Servd’s *clone/import* between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to
> Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
> <https://servd.host/docs/assets?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
>

On Nov 10, 2025 at 12:59 PM -0700, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>, wrote:
>  Hi Shaun,
>
> Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.
>
> The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting together:
> There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for each.
> A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)
> Where to edit: Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
> Why: Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
> Simple steps
>
> 1. > In Production, open the entry → Create Draft → review (use Preview) → Publish when approved.
> 2. > If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior Revision at any time. Craft CMS: Entries
>
> When not to do this: If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.
> Rollback (content): Restore the previous Revision of the entry, or restore a Production DB backup if needed.
> Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)
> Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production, practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.
> Steps
>
> 1. > Staging → set its bundle to match Production (code parity). Bundles are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
> 2. > Clone Production → Staging (DB + assets). This overwrites Staging; make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
> 3. > Make/review content changes on Staging.
> 4. > Clone Staging → Production (DB + assets) to launch.
>
> Timing: Do this in a short window off-hours. The clone replaces Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm. (Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)
> Rollback (content via clone): Restore Production from Servd backup or re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
> B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — no schema
> Policy: Production does not auto-build from merges. We promote the tested Staging bundle to Production.
> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>
> 1. > Open a PR into staging; merge when approved.
> 2. > Servd builds a new bundle for Staging from that commit; test the site on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
> 3. > In Servd → Production → assign the same Staging bundle (Deploy/Assign Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
> 4. > Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op; caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
>
> Rollback (code): In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous known-good bundle.
> CLI path (for devs)
> # create/update feature and push git checkout -b feature/xyz
> # (edit files) git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ" git push origin feature/xyz # open PR → merge to staging git checkout staging git pull git merge --no-ff feature/xyz git push origin staging
> Then test Staging and assign the Staging bundle to Production in Servd. (No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
> C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)
> These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.). They must move via Project Config and migrations.
> Important defaults: In Production, allowAdminChanges should be false so schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS: Project Config
> Click-only path (GitHub App users)
>
> 1. > Make the settings/field changes on Staging CMS (or local with admin changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
> 2. > Commit & merge to staging; Servd builds a bundle.
> 3. > Staging deploy runs your Post-Deploy Tasks: craft up (migrations + project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
> 4. > In Servd, assign the same bundle to Production. The same Post-Deploy Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.
>
> Rollback (schema):
>
> • > Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous bundle.
> • > If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the Production DB backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.
>
> CLI path (for devs)
> # Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)
> # Commit project config & composer updates
> git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
> git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
> git push origin staging
> # Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging bundle to build and deploy
> On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually (rare):
>
> • > php craft up --interactive=0
> • > php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
>
> When Staging passes QA, assign the same bundle to Production (Servd UI).
> D) Assets (practical note)
> Use the Servd Asset Platform + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s clone/import between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > AR-68: I think we might have (unfortunately) opened up a can of worms on this one. If you look at the scholarships page, there are also two sidebar items that are in Spanish. Since the heading button text use a plain text field, I assume the current method isn’t an option. Potential solutions I can think of are:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > What are your thoughts on this? I’m looking for the best solution that satisfies the WCAG 2.2 AA spec, doesn’t muddy the editing process, while also not creating a ton of work.

Date: Mon, 10 Nov 2025 12:59:26 -0700
From: Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>

Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

Hi Shaun,

Thanks for your patience while I had family in town last week.

The following is a snippet of the Aspen Project End Review I'm putting
together:

There are four kinds of changes and the paths are slightly different for
each.
A) Normal content updates (Aspen team)

*Where to edit:* Production, using Drafts/Revisions and Publish when ready.
*Why:* Craft’s drafts/revisions are built for safe, reviewable content
edits on the live site; schema/config isn’t touched. Craft CMS: Revisions
<https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/drafts-revisions.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>


*Simple steps*

   1.

   In Production, open the entry → *Create Draft* → review (use Preview) →
   *Publish* when approved.
   2.

   If you need an extra safety net, restore a prior *Revision* at any
time. Craft
   CMS: Entries
   <https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/reference/element-types/entries.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

*When not to do this:* If Production content is corrupted or must rehearse
a complex content launch offline, you can use the clone workflow below.

*Rollback (content):* Restore the previous *Revision* of the entry, or
restore a Production DB backup if needed.
------------------------------
Optional: “Clone & rehearse” content workflow (off-hours)

Use this only when a rehearsal is needed: make Staging match Production,
practice changes, then launch the exact reviewed content back to Production.

*Steps*

   1.

   Staging → set its *bundle* to match Production (code parity). Bundles
   are immutable code snapshots tied to Git commits. servd.host: Bundles
   <https://servd.host/docs/whats-a-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
   2.

   *Clone Production → Staging* (DB + assets). This *overwrites Staging*;
   make/confirm backups first. servd.host: Cloning an Environment
   <https://servd.host/docs/cloning-an-environment?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
   3.

   Make/review content changes on Staging.
   4.

   *Clone Staging → Production* (DB + assets) to launch.

*Timing:* Do this in a short window *off-hours*. The clone replaces
Production’s DB/assets and can temporarily impact UX while caches warm.
(Servd’s clone is a destructive copy; plan a brief content freeze.)

*Rollback (content via clone):* Restore Production from Servd backup or
re-clone from a known-good environment. Craft CMS: Hosting & Deployment
<https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/deploy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
------------------------------
B) Code-only changes (templates/Vue/CSS/JS) — *no schema*

*Policy:* Production does *not* auto-build from merges. We promote the *tested
Staging bundle* to Production.
Click-only path (GitHub App users)

   1.

   Open a PR into *staging*; merge when approved.
   2.

   Servd builds a new *bundle* for Staging from that commit; test the site
   on Staging. servd.host: New Bundle
   <https://servd.host/docs/create-a-new-bundle?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
   3.

   In Servd → *Production* → assign *the same Staging bundle* (Deploy/Assign
   Bundle). This puts the exact tested code live.
   4.

   Post-Deploy Tasks run (craft up isn’t needed here, but it will no-op;
   caches are cleared). servd.host: Post Deploy Tasks
   <https://servd.host/docs/post-deploy-tasks?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

*Rollback (code):* In Servd → Production → re-assign the previous
known-good bundle.
CLI path (for devs)

# create/update feature and push
git checkout -b feature/xyz
# (edit files)
git add -A && git commit -m "Feature XYZ"
git push origin feature/xyz
# open PR → merge to staging
git checkout staging
git pull
git merge --no-ff feature/xyz
git push origin staging

Then test Staging and *assign the Staging bundle to Production* in Servd.
(No project-config apply needed for code-only work.)
------------------------------
C) Schema/Settings/Plugin changes (Project Config + migrations)

These are structural CMS changes (fields, sections, plugin settings, etc.).
They must move via *Project Config* and migrations.

*Important defaults:* In Production, allowAdminChanges should be *false* so
schema isn’t edited directly. Changes flow via YAML and deploys. Craft CMS:
Project Config
<https://craftcms.com/docs/5.x/system/project-config.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com>
Click-only path (GitHub App users)

   1.

   Make the settings/field changes on *Staging CMS* (or local with admin
   changes enabled). Craft writes them to config/project/*.yaml.
   2.

   Commit & merge to *staging*; Servd builds a bundle.
   3.

   Staging deploy runs your *Post-Deploy Tasks*: craft up (migrations +
   project-config apply) then craft clear-caches/all. Verify Staging works.
   4.

   In Servd, *assign the same bundle* to *Production*. The same Post-Deploy
   Tasks run there, applying schema and clearing caches.

*Rollback (schema):*

   -

   Revert the YAML/composer commit → rebuild bundle → assign previous
   bundle.
   -

   If DB migrations weren’t backward-compatible, restore the *Production DB*
    backup, then re-assign the prior bundle.

CLI path (for devs)

# Make changes on staging (or local with allowAdminChanges true)#
Commit project config & composer updates
git add config/project composer.json composer.lock
git commit -m "Schema: add field X / plugin update"
git push origin staging# Merge PR if needed, then wait for Staging
bundle to build and deploy

On Staging, Post-Deploy Tasks will run automatically. To run manually
(rare):

   -

   php craft up --interactive=0
   -

   php craft clear-caches/all Craft CMS Stack Exchange
   <https://craftcms.stackexchange.com/questions/41038/run-craft-up-command-in-deployment-pipeline-without-prompts?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

When Staging passes QA, *assign the same bundle to Production* (Servd UI).
------------------------------
D) Assets (practical note)

Use the *Servd Asset Platform* + Craft (uploads, bulk import), and Servd’s
*clone/import* between environments. Avoid ad-hoc FTP to Production; keep
bulk or repair tasks developer-only. servd.host: Assets
<https://servd.host/docs/assets?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > What are your thoughts on this? I’m looking for the best solution that satisfies the WCAG 2.2 AA spec, doesn’t muddy the editing process, while also not creating a ton of work.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > AR-68: I think we might have (unfortunately) opened up a can of worms on this one. If you look at the scholarships page, there are also two sidebar items that are in Spanish. These items use the CTA block in craft and are designed to contain an image, heading, text content, and button. Since the heading button text use a plain text field, I assume the current method isn’t an option. Potential solutions I can think of are:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. This would solve the immediate issue, but feels like we’d be opening a can of worms since there’s other blocks on the site this may need to be built into.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > What are your thoughts on this? I’m looking for the best solution that satisfies the WCAG 2.2 AA spec, doesn’t muddy the editing process, while also not creating a ton of work.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Build the option to assign the lang as a field within the CTA that applies to the entire CTA block of code. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. A more streamlined approach I think I favor is to force the declaration of the language that applies to the entire page (or at least anything rendered inside the <main> element, so that we can exclude the header and footer). My proposal for this method would be to build a language option for any content page on the site (ignoring other templated pages for now) so that the code would output something like <main class="relative" id=“mainContent” lang=“es”>. This would mean we’d need to split the current scholarships page into two versions: English and Spanish, but it would sidestep the issue of needing to specify langagues on such a granular level across many points in the system.
