I know we’d talked previously about payment upon completion, but given the fact you’ve definitely put in a lot of hours and the work, I feel, is going well, I could definitely arrange getting a check to you if that would help?

On a related note, with the use of the dev environment, I’ve been able to get a little more comfortable in the website’s code environment and make more edits on my own that I was originally was thinking possible. If you’re at a point where you need to scale back your work on this project, I may be able to step in and try my hand at fixing some of the remaining items, if needed. The areas I’d still need the most help with are edits that delve into the Vue components, especially the calendar. I was able to add focus to the calendar items and open the modal via keyboard (taking care of AR-41) but I’m only somewhat knowledgeable in javascript, so adding labels, etc. to the existing markup that references other variables and functions is where I tend to waste a lot of time over misunderstandings in syntax, etc.

To help prioritize the remaining work, here’s a rough list of relative priorities. I’ve noted items I feel comfortable trying to solve first, if you need to scale back here...

1. Focus trap on modals
2. Skip to content link - (I’m pretty sure I can handle this one)
3. Main Navigation - Learning what I did from AR-41, I may be able to solve this one as well if you’d like me try?
4. Activity Tables:
    a. Can't switch between table tabs with keyboard - I may also be able to take a stab at this one since I’m assuming it’s similar to AR-41.
    b. Aria labels on buttons - I can probably figure this one out as well
5. Calendar (Need to figure out how to properly label cells, and/or if elements can become a table)
I want to get a little more feedback on what “properly labeled” means in this context, so I’ve reached out to BeAccessible for more info. In our initial review, Lindsey mentioned that she’d mainly been focused on the lack of labeling for when the calendar is filtered and content is updated. You can see that in our recorded audit review meeting at around the 1:18:00 mark: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1F7CxtxZ3aILSkdrhglLlTIXJ7fSq7FXH/view?usp=drive_link.

I was also able to fix AR-16 along the way, so there’s at least one more off of the list!

Recognizing that sometimes two people working at the same time on the same code can be like having too many cooks in the kitchen, I’d value your honest opinion on whether I’d be getting in the way, or helping. My main goal is try to reduce the financial/time burden this has become on you by trying to absorb what I can myself since it’s unlikely I’ll be able to secure any additional budget for the work.

As always, please feel free to be open about any thoughts/concerns/questions you have and also feel free to call anytime.

> > > > > > > Basically, what's going on is that it's looking for a table called userpreferences and can't find it.
> > > > > > > The only codebase reference to userpreferences is in seed_db.sql, this means:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > • The userpreferences table was never created in the active database, or
> > > > > > > • It was dropped at some point and not recreated.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > What This Means for the Error
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't exist.
> > > > > > >     • It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g., language settings, UI settings).
> > > > > > >     • Since the table is missing, the query fails, causing the error you see.
> > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > The table was probably created manually at some point but is not included in active migrations.
> > > > > > >     • If it were a CraftCMS core table, it would have been recreated automatically.
> > > > > > >     • Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a custom migration or a plugin that is no longer active.
> > > > > > >

> > > > > > > • Formie

>> Basically, what's going on is that it's looking for a table called
>> userpreferences and can't find it.
>>
>> The only codebase reference to userpreferences is in *seed_db.sql*, this
>> means:
>>
>>    - The userpreferences table *was never created* in the active
>>    database, or
>>    - It was *dropped at some point* and not recreated.
>>
>> *What This Means for the Error*
>>
>>    1.
>>
>>    *CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't
>>    exist.*
>>    - It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g.,
>>       language settings, UI settings).
>>       - Since the table is missing, the query *fails*, causing the error
>>       you see.
>>    2.
>>
>>    *The table was probably created manually at some point but is not
>>    included in active migrations.*
>>    - If it were a *CraftCMS core table*, it would have been recreated
>>       automatically.
>>       - Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a *custom
>>       migration or a plugin* that is no longer active.
>>

2025-01-31 18:58:22 [web.WARNING] [application] Request context:

Basically, what's going on is that it's looking for a table called
userpreferences and can't find it.

The only codebase reference to userpreferences is in *seed_db.sql*, this
means:

   - The userpreferences table *was never created* in the active database,
   or
   - It was *dropped at some point* and not recreated.

*What This Means for the Error*

   1.

   *CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't
   exist.*
   - It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g.,
      language settings, UI settings).
      - Since the table is missing, the query *fails*, causing the error
      you see.
   2.

   *The table was probably created manually at some point but is not
   included in active migrations.*
   - If it were a *CraftCMS core table*, it would have been recreated
      automatically.
      - Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a *custom
      migration or a plugin* that is no longer active.

My inclination would be that it's an issue with one of these plugins:

   - SEOmatic
   - Redactor
   - Formie

If I had to guess, I'd bet on Redactor as the offending plugin.

The good news is that this should resolve with the package updates we have
planned.

Do you feel like this is pressing enough to need an immediate response or
will it be okay to resolve as I get there in the next month?

Hi Eric,

Thanks for looking into it.

To see the error, you’ll need to go to the Curling record within the activities collection (not the drop-in curling record under classes/events). Within the activity entry, there’s a drop-in tab with the old drop-in item de-activated. Re-activate that and I think the error should re-appear. However, due to caching, it may not show for you in your browser. To force everything to rebuild, here’s what I did:

1. Disable the caching in production in Servd (just a toggle switch in the settings); re-sync.
2. Turn on the drop-in record within the curling activity.
3. Use the cache-clearing tools in Craft Utilities.
4. Clear your browser cache by completely deleting all cookies and data for aspenrecreation.com.
5. Refresh page.
6. Check Servd error logs.

With any luck, you should see that the calendar loading stalls on the front end, and a PHP error shows in the Servd logs.

Apologies for not being clearer with that in my email last night.

We’re headed off to a family reunion today through Monday. I’ll keep an eye on this thread and try my best to respond if you have any additional questions.

If you wouldn’t mind, please be sure to set any entries and Servd settings back when you’ve concluded your investigation.

Thanks!

On the other issues:

   - The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page. I've
   sorted it out now--the "showNews" logic just needed to be tweaked a bit.
   - In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing and
   this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is in
   place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't resolving
   currently and you're right that production should improve it some.
   - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from
   1.9:
      - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
      in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
      switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
      × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
      while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
      - For instance, the old system
         - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
           <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
         - The new system:
         - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
           <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
                p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
         - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have things
      restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
      definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
      tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
      want now.
   - The accessibility checker issues:
      - *Four landmark issues*:
         - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
         - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity Calendar
         </span>
         - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
         element to main navigation, main navigation items and
"utility navigation
         items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
         aria-label
      - *Modal Accessible Name*:
         - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label fallback
         with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID
down to the
         component children which should ensure consistency for Screen Readers.
      - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
      navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
      The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a
semantic nav
      element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the
roles and this
      should be clean now.

All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load
times and placeholder usage.

>>>>
>>>>    1. Got it. That color is corrected.
>>>>    2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on
>>>>    this last--now that is.
>>>>    3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
>>>>    4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so
>>>>    thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple
>>>>    naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was
>>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used
>>>>    focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use
>>>>    the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
>>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
>>>>
>>>> Other notes:
>>>>
>>>>    1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font
>>>>    size was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I
>>>>    see the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
>>>>    gray-600.

>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-*
>>>    as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-*
>>>    directly and the focus is implied.
>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.

> > 3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
> > 4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.
> > 5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
> > 6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
> >
> > Other notes:
> >

> your points:
>
>    1. Got it. That color is corrected.
>    2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on this
>    last--now that is.
>    3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
>    4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so
>    thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple
>    naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was
>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-*
>    as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-*
>    directly and the focus is implied.
>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
>
> Other notes:
>
>    1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font size
>    was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I see
>    the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
>    gray-600.
>    2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is now

>    3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm going

Okay, thank you again for the feedback.

There was a lingering "redactor" reference in the project.yaml file that I
corrected. Dev mostly reflects local now--the dev database is slightly
different from local but this isn't crucial since the database and assets
are going to update to production anyway. So it's safe now to continue with
your points:

   1. Got it. That color is corrected.
   2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on this
   last--now that is.
   3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
   4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks
   for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming
   convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and
   in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to
   fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of
   !important to override variables for particular instances which would
   occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner.
   To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to
   avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a
   different naming convention you prefer.
   5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as
   inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-*
   directly and the focus is implied.
   6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
   reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

Other notes:

   1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font size
   was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I see
   the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
   gray-600.
   2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is now
   fixed.
   3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm going
   through but using the predefined sizes--e.g. outline-thick, text-sm,
   etc.--don't seem to be exactly right so this is just a fine-tuning note
   that shouldn't affect accessibility.

Just pushed the corrections to dev so that should be updated within a few
minutes

> > 3. The menu items seem to be using a different color for the focus outline. Dev uses a value of #0f5d22, which is a dark green. In and of itself, that’s fine. The confusing part is that the value comes from "--outline-gray”, so I’m not sure why that value is outputting a green color instead of gray.
> >
> > 4. The focus outlines for the news filters, news items, and blog posts is gray instead of blue. Both meet contrast, so it’s not an accessibility issue, just a minor one I noticed.
> >
> > 5. There’s a small white gap below the thumbnail of news items. Not an accessibility issue, just some extra spacing that appears to have been introduced somewhere down the line that makes those seem a bit untidy.

==== EMAIL 349 ====
Date: Tue, 26 Aug 2025 16:37:23 -0600
From: Shaun Cooney | Monument Graphics <shaun@monumentgraphics.com>
To:   Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>
Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

Hi Eric,

Thanks for the video. I’m sorry you had to rebuild so much of the code manually.

Overall, this is looking much better. There are still some minor visual differences I’ll note below. The more important items to address would be:

1. The focus outline color for the social icons in the footer needs to match the icon hover color. It currently does not have enough contrast. I believe that should be "--outline-black” –› #181919.
2. I do believe the arrow issues will need to be corrected on mobile, as that’ll come up in the validation.
3. The callout text in the gray box below the slider is missing. This appears tied to a redactor field that wasn’t updated. You can find that text field under ‘Entries › Singles › Homepage’.

Other, less pressing differences I noticed:

3. The menu items seem to be using a different color for the focus outline. The current one meets contrast, so this doesn’t present an accessibility issue, but it may cause a little confusion in the code. Production uses a value of #27871c defined via a CSS rule. Dev uses a value of #0f5d22, which is a dark green. In and of itself, that’s fine. The confusing part is that the value comes from "--outline-gray”, so I’m not sure why that value is outputting a green color instead of gray.

4. The focus outlines for the news filters, news items, and blog posts is gray instead of blue. Both meet contrast, so it’s not an accessibility issue, just a minor one I noticed.

5. There’s a small white gap below the thumbnail of news items. Not an accessibility issue, just some extra spacing that appears to have been introduced somewhere down the line that makes those seem a bit untidy.


I realize the last three are very minor and you’ve spent tons of time already, so if things are currently set up for me to make edits to the code, push to GitHub, and rebuild the bundle in Serv’d as we did before, I can plan on making those changes. Otherwise, if we need to revisit that process of how I make changes, please let me know.

Thanks,

Shaun Cooney } MONUMENT GRAPHICS | DESIGN + WEB
PO Box 299, Fruita, CO 81521
(970) 242-4311 • MonumentGraphics.com

Hey Shaun,

Thanks for the feedback.

That's not surprising. I had to restructure and rewrite the vast majority
of the front end code since Tailwind 4 is so different from 1.9, Pinia
storage is very different from Vuex and Vue3 has syntactic changes from
Vue2, plus the required update from Node 16 to Node 20.18. Since very
little of the original code has actually survived this update it's amazing
that I've made it look so close. 🤣

I'm sending a video with the side by side comparison after I've made a
couple of updates. Let me know if you're seeing the same things.
 aspen-side-by-side.mp4

page visited, when I fix this, the activity pages stop filtering and show
all events.

Quick question with that: do you want the events for each week to show for
the full week as they currently do in production or do you want the events
to be removed by day? (e.g. on a Wednesday, events for Sunday, Monday,
Tuesday won't show.) I have it set to the latter currently--an
unintentional change while figuring out the filtering--but I can easily
switch it back. Just wanted to check which functionality works better for
Aspen.

Once I sort out the filters, the calendar should be 100%--that's what I'm
looking to wrap up this week. I'm going through our past checklists and I'm
about 60% through them.

I still have an eye to releasing a functional version as soon as possible.

I do have some improvements I haven't pushed to dev yet so let me know if
you need to see the latest.

On a side note, Joseph Center is trying to raise funds to keep their doors
open so I'm helping with the technology and marketing aspects of that.
Every other spare moment I have I'm putting toward wrapping up Aspen--I
know we're all ready for it to be done and I'm using every resource I have
available to make that happen this month.

Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

To prepare, I’ve done a deeper dive comparing the two sites and came up with the following list. I’ve assigned a star rating indicating relative priority. The more asterisks before an item, the more important it is from an operating/accessibility standpoint. Hopefully, most of these are relatively minor:


NATURAL RESOURCES & FORESTRY PAGES
1) ***Template errors - cannot view pages

NAVIGATION
2) **Top three items in black text are missing their previous focus states
3) **Elements (input, search, close) within search are missing the previous focus states
4) Search results are missing thumbnail images (possibly due to this being a subdomain?)

MODALS
5) *If I visit the homepage, close the modal, then visit another page and return to the homepage, the modal loads in the last position I was in (i.e., displays an individual item, rather than the entire list). Can we set this to “forget” the user’s last interaction and load it fresh each time? Also curious if there’s any way to limit loading this to once per user session? (Only need info regarding this last query, please don’t make a change yet).
6) **When navigating to view more info about an item or "go back" within the modals, the focus isn't initially set, and my screen reader reads as though it's on a new page, rather than a changed modal on the same page.
7) *If the page is refreshed while a modal is open, the focus state seems to highlight a random area from the last state the modal was at and the screen reader will read out content that doesn’t match what’s on screen.
8) All text is currently centered. Can we set this back to left-aligned as before?

FOOTER
9) **Subscribe popup –› Focus states and error styles are missing when using keyboard.

CALENDARS
10) ***If using keyboard to open an event modal, the focus correctly goes to the close button. However, if the Enter key is used to close the modal, it immediately reopens it and forms a never-ending loop that can't be escaped unless the user knows to use the space key.
11) **Focus states for expanded calendar filters are missing their previous focus states
12) “Filter Calendar” heading is showing on non-filterable calendars (i.e., on activity or facility pages). There’s a chance this may have been my doing since it exists on both sites, so if you feel this is out of scope, please let me know.

CONTENT CONTAINERS
13) All pages with <div class=“container”> are narrower than before. Can we adjust the width to match?
14) Homepage: News items are stretching too wide. Looks like the div with the container class is missing from this section.

BLUE CALLOUTS (Sitewide)
15) *Button focus states need to be restored for contrast.

HERO SLIDERS
16) **Slide controls are missing their previous focus states
17) Load time for initial image seems very slow (might be due to environment caching?)
18) *Hero images are shorter on homepage & Parks Dept. Landing page; Hero on Parks landing page is exceedingly tall (https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/aspen-area-parks).

STATUS UPDATES
19) **Title shifts from stacked on top to floating left when opened (I believe this is a bug from our first round of work).

NEWS ITEMS
20) *Screen readers need to provide notification when content changes via filters

PHOTO GALLERIES
21) **not keyboard operable (https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/activities/full-day-camp/youth)

ACTIVITY PAGES
22) Is there an easy way to allow keyboard users to skip over the activity tables? BeAccessible was suggesting we do this.

------------------------------

OTHER MINOR DIFFERENCES
23) The focus states (text color changes and outline colors/styles) for news filter controls, passes, attractions (Rec Centers), news items, policies, sidebar links, and parks/trails/fields grids don't match the previous version
24) A-Z Guide: need to clean up focus states around the letters (appears I missed this the first go-around, so I can put this on my plate if needed).

It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

>>>>    accessibility scan issues. In the calendar, the font size has been reduced.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Another update for this week: definitely making progress! Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Another update for this week: definitely making progress! Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Another update for this week: definitely making progress!
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> convention for a smoother transition.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> But since you work in the Tailwind config too I want to

Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

Hi Eric,

Thanks as always for the update. I hope you’ve had a chance to enjoy a bit of a longer weekend.

Hopefully, I’m not the bearer of bad news here, but unfortunately, I’m still coming across quite a few mismatches with the dev site. Luckily, I think what I’m seeing page-by-page can mostly be corrected on a global level and many of the issues are probably connected. I’ve only performed a cursory review so far, but here’s what I’m seeing at first glance:

1. Image aspect ratios/heights: Almost anywhere images have been cropped, I’m seeing inconsistencies vs production. This includes the hero sliders on the homepage and parks landing pages, as well as the thumbnails for the lists of parks, trails, and open spaces on those respective pages. In addition, the thumbnails for attractions on the facility pages (Aspen Rec Center, etc.) aren’t being cropped at 1:1 as before, and anywhere the gallery block was used (such as on the Aspen Rec Center page), the images are being cropped and placed differently.
2. Container spacing: Throughout most of the site, the overall width of the content area has been reduced, and the gutter between columns is often missing. Please see the Aspen Rec Center page on dev vs production for comparison. In a few places where text is supposed to stretch across the majority of the screen, it is not (https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/more-info/about).
3. Text sizing & spacing: Most prose/body text looks like the line height has been decreased, which will probably trigger some accessibility scan issues. In the calendar, the font size has been reduced. In the sidebars, some of the formatting for headers has been lost. Please see the Aspen Rec Center page again for a comparison.
4. In-page Status Updates: The header for status updates doesn’t seem to be showing on pages where those are present (e.g. Red Brick Rec Center page, youth climbing)
5. Fitness Wellness Error: The adult Fitness & Wellness page is not rendering correctly. Somehow, it looks like all CSS data is missing from this page.
6. Mobile-sized focus states on desktop: These were the ones I had to add in since it’s possible to zoom in on the site on desktop and trigger mobile styles. It looks like these have been lost in the dev version.
7. Spacing of News Items on Homepage: On the dev site, the width of the container for these appears to be much wider than before. Looks odd on really big screens.

As I look at those items closer, the list doesn’t seem too horrible. Page-by-page, things look a little disjointed to me, but I think correcting the image, spacing, and text issues will clean up the vast majority of differences I’m seeing. As a point of reference, here are some good pages to pull up side-by-side on the dev site vs production to help spot the differences I’m seeing:

HOME: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/
ARC: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/aspen-recreation-center
RED BRICK: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/red-brick-recreation-center
YOUTH ACTIVITIES: Climbing, Swimming, and any of the camp pages are usually good litmus tests
ADULT ACTIVITIES: Fitness & Wellness, Hockey, and Climbing are usually the best pages to check
PARKS DEPT HOME: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails
PARKS LANDING: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/aspen-area-parks
TRAILS LANDING: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/aspen-area-trails
OPEN SPACES LANDING: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/open-spaces
FORESTRY & NATURAL RESOURCES: https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/natural-resources-forestry
RENTAL INFO: https://www.aspenrecreation.com/rec-centers/rental-reservation-info

A couple of quick notes that may help you in the process of further debugging:

• The parks department pages for individual parks, fields, or forestry info are good ones to check for sidebar text styling issues. They use the sidebars in that department, as do the activity pages.
• The Red Brick, ARC, and Adult Fitness/Wellness pages use the widest variety of technologies. They’re usually the pages I default to when needing to compare versions.
• Adult & Youth Hockey is one of the only activities that seems to use leagues anymore. I usually check that page to look for issues with the activity table tabs.
• Basketball & Pickleball are often the only activities that use the Drop-Ins feature, so I always check those as well.
• I’ve found page-by-page comparisons somewhat difficult since the content often differs. If there’s a fast way to sync the databases, I’d recommend we do that so we can better compare apples to apples.


I hope that helps pinpoint what I’m seeing. If you’d like to do a screenshare or call just let me know!

point so I think I can call the update portion complete with a couple of
caveats.

with the accessibility checks I'm doing now. It looks like Tailwind

throw !important on each of those and get it back.

Second, if the past is any indication there's always something more that
pops up so I wouldn't call it production ready yet but at least ready for
Quality Assurance tests.

Let me know what you see whenever you can.

I'm still working on things but as of today I've switched to accessibility
focus.

I'm starting to feel happy about the progress, which makes me nervous. 😂

Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >

It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

styling.

again later today to let you know we have a full 1:1 match with production
style-wise.

me know if you need that higher in priority.

Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Another update for this week: definitely making progress! Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> hang-ups).
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> support Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>  vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> here's some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> you apprised.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> On Thu, Jan 2, 2025 at 12:28 PM Eric Phifer <
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> eric@ericphiferllc.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Shaun,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Happy New Year and I hope your Christmas was good.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> I've started back in on the Aspen work, beginning
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> with updating to Vue3. I plan to work on Aspen W, Th, F until it's complete
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> (aiming for the end of February at the latest and praying there's no
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> hang-ups).
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> support Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> here's some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

The principle being that a reverse outline was used for outlines appearing on top of a colored background. The footer links under more info would be a good example of one place this is used.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> support Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> here's some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management)
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

Before I wasn't getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography. Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention for a smoother transition.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> support Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>  or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management)
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). >>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management)
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> I've started back in on the Aspen work, beginning with
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> updating to Vue3. I plan to work on Aspen W, Th, F until it's complete
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> (aiming for the end of February at the latest and praying there's no
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> hang-ups).
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vue 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Shaun,
