>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Happy New Year and I hope your Christmas was good.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> I've started back in on the Aspen work, beginning with
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> updating to Vue3. I plan to work on Aspen W, Th, F until it's complete
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> (aiming for the end of February at the latest and praying there's no
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> hang-ups).
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> some options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

Shaun,

Another update for this week: definitely making progress! Before I wasn't
getting any styles to show up in Dev but now I have about 1600 styling
rules applying - this still isn't anywhere near the ~34k rules applying in
production. The trouble is that Tailwind 4 decided to drop
tailwind.config.js - they still support it but I'm finding it's actually
making the build more difficult to keep. So I've migrated all the theme
sections from tailwind.config into app.pcss under the @theme directive.

One of the advantages of this is Tailwind now automatically searches the
entire codebase for styling. However, a downside is the typography.
Previously the @tailwindcss/typography plugin added the prose class and
Aspen had a list of css being applied on various elements, but now
typography is not yet supported in v4. It looks like we can gain a similar
effect by adding our own variables while using the prose naming convention
for a smoother transition.

But since you work in the Tailwind config too I want to make sure this is
set up in a way that makes sense to you and get your thoughts on the
Typography issue. I'm attaching the pcss file.

Let me know if you have any questions and feel free to call if that's
easier.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> 3 *natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you
>>>>>>>>>>>>>> apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling
>>>>>>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing
>>>>>>>>>>>>> loader and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively.
>>>>>>>>>>>>> This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork
>>>>>>>>>>>>> called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to
>>>>>>>>>>>>> Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for
>>>>>>>>>>>>> future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like
>>>>>>>>>>>>> it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

If you need any other information, please let me know and I’ll dig in to see what I can find.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling
>>>>>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader
>>>>>>>>>>>> and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively.
>>>>>>>>>>>> This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork
>>>>>>>>>>>> called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging
>>>>>>>>>>>>    Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like
>>>>>>>>>>>>    Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option
>>>>>>>>>>>>    ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia
>>>>>>>>>>>> (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>>>>>>>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>>>>>>>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling
>>>>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader
>>>>>>>>>>> and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively.
>>>>>>>>>>> This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork
>>>>>>>>>>> called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging
>>>>>>>>>>>    Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like
>>>>>>>>>>>    Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option
>>>>>>>>>>>    ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or
>>>>>>>>>>> build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented,
>>>>>>>>>>> actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This
>>>>>>>>>>> option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established
>>>>>>>>>>> tools.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia
>>>>>>>>>>> (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>>>>>>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>>>>>>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

>>>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader
>>>>>>>>>> and progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively.
>>>>>>>>>> This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork
>>>>>>>>>> called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its
>>>>>>>>>> long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is
>>>>>>>>>> referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the
>>>>>>>>>> app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may
>>>>>>>>>> just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act
>>>>>>>>>> without your approval.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
>>>>>>>>>>     provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or
>>>>>>>>>>    Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures
>>>>>>>>>>    full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build
>>>>>>>>>> a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively
>>>>>>>>>> maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may
>>>>>>>>>> necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia
>>>>>>>>>> (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>>>>>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>>>>>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>>> This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork
>>>>>>>>> called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its

>>>>>>>>> without your approval.

>>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
>>>>>>>>>    provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or
>>>>>>>>>    Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures
>>>>>>>>>    full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build
>>>>>>>>> a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively
>>>>>>>>> maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>>>> Shaun,

>>>>>>>> I've started back in on the Aspen work, beginning with updating to
>>>>>>>> Vue3. I plan to work on Aspen W, Th, F until it's complete (aiming for the
>>>>>>>> end of February at the latest and praying there's no hang-ups).
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling
>>>>>>>> package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your
>>>>>>>> thoughts on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and
>>>>>>>> progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively. This
>>>>>>>> presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>>>  vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term
>>>>>>>> viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced
>>>>>>>> is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file
>>>>>>>> and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to
>>>>>>>> remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your
>>>>>>>> approval.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some
>>>>>>>> options for that:
>>>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
>>>>>>>>    provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or
>>>>>>>>    Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures
>>>>>>>>    full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a
>>>>>>>> bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively
>>>>>>>> maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may
>>>>>>>> necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia
>>>>>>>> (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>>>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>>>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts on when you have a chance:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > vue-wait
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress states in Vue 2, does not support Vue 3 natively. This presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security have not been fully vetted.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your approval.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for that:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Adopt vue-wait-vue3:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Implement a Custom Loading Solution:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full control, security, and alignment with project needs.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

>>>>>> end of February at the latest and praying there's no hang-ups).
>>>>>>
>>>>>> There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package
>>>>>> migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts
>>>>>> on when you have a chance:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> *vue-wait*
>>>>>>
>>>>>> The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and
>>>>>> progress states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively. This
>>>>>> presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>>>  vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term
>>>>>> viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced
>>>>>> is in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file
>>>>>> and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to
>>>>>> remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your
>>>>>> approval.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else
>>>>>> statements which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options
>>>>>> for that:
>>>>>> ------------------------------
>>>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    1.
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is
>>>>>>    designed for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution
>>>>>>    with minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security
>>>>>>    and maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>>>    2.
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>>>
>>>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
>>>>>>    provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex.
>>>>>>    While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full
>>>>>>    control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a
>>>>>> bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively
>>>>>> maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may
>>>>>> necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the
>>>>>> Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

>>>> presents a challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called
>>>>  vue-wait-vue3 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term
>>>> viability and security have not been fully vetted.
>>>>
>>>> However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is
>>>> in the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file
>>>> and that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to
>>>> remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your
>>>> approval.
>>>>
>>>> It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements
>>>> which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
>>>> lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.
>>>>
>>>> If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options
>>>> for that:
>>>> ------------------------------
>>>> Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:
>>>>
>>>>    1.
>>>>
>>>>    *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*
>>>>
>>>>    Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed
>>>>    for Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with
>>>>    minimal changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and
>>>>    maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
>>>>    2.
>>>>
>>>>    *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*
>>>>
>>>>    Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
>>>>    provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex.
>>>>    While requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full
>>>>    control, security, and alignment with project needs.
>>>>    3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *
>>>>
>>>> Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a
>>>> bespoke loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively
>>>> maintained, and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may
>>>> necessitate refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.
>>>>
>>>> Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the
>>>> Vue docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
>>>> maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
>>>> be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.
>>>>
>>>> There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

Shaun,

Happy New Year and I hope your Christmas was good.

I've started back in on the Aspen work, beginning with updating to Vue3. I
plan to work on Aspen W, Th, F until it's complete (aiming for the end of
February at the latest and praying there's no hang-ups).

There's been quite a bit of progress already as I'm handling package
migration one at a time. There is one package that I'll need your thoughts
on when you have a chance:

*vue-wait*

The original vue-wait package, widely used for managing loader and progress
states in Vue 2, does *not support Vue 3 *natively. This presents a
challenge when transitioning to Vue 3. A community fork called vue-wait-vue3
 claims to provide compatibility, but its long-term viability and security
have not been fully vetted.

However, I've searched the code and the only place it is referenced is in
the wait.js file, which in turn is only referenced in the app.ts file and
that is currently commented out so if it's unused we may just want to
remove it. I just didn't want to perform a destructive act without your
approval.

It looks like the loading states are handled via v-if/v-else statements
which I think is a good way to handle loading states - it's both
lightweight and accessible. See calendar--events.vue for an example.

If you want to keep it for later implementation, here's some options for
that:
------------------------------
Top 3 Options for Addressing the Issue:

   1.

   *Adopt vue-wait-vue3:*

   Use the community-maintained fork vue-wait-vue3, which is designed for
   Vue 3 compatibility. This option provides a drop-in solution with minimal
   changes to the existing code but introduces potential security and
   maintenance concerns due to its unofficial nature.
   2.

   *Implement a Custom Loading Solution:*

   Replace vue-wait with a custom Vue 3 solution leveraging Vue's
   provide/inject API or state management tools like Pinia or Vuex. While
   requiring more development effort upfront, this option ensures full
   control, security, and alignment with project needs.
   3. *Evaluate and Migrate to Alternative Libraries: *

Explore modern alternatives such as vue-loading-overlay or build a bespoke
loader component. These libraries are well-documented, actively maintained,
and designed with Vue 3 compatibility in mind. This option may necessitate
refactoring but ensures reliance on established tools.

Just a heads up, I'm migrating Vuex (state management) to Pinia (the Vue
docs call it Vuex 5 and recommend Pinia over Vuex 4 for future
maintainability). I've checked the documentation and it looks like it will
be a smoother transition than staying with Vuex 4.

There's no change for Aspen on this, just keeping you apprised.

Date: Mon, 8 Apr 2024 12:35:07 -0600
From: Shaun Cooney <shaun@monumentgraphics.com>

Subject: Re: Accordions

Hi Eric,

The headers have proven to be quite a tangled web. I still need to do more work on those, so please keep in touch regarding safe times for me to work on those that don’t interfere with your work. I’m also chipping away at the Redactor config. One of the pain points on the site was that Mark several version of the Page/Content Builder block and placed several blocks in each of those, but many don’t work or behave unexpectedly, making it a real challenge for the staff to know what’s “safe” to use and where. Many of these blocks use specific heading levels, so while I’m in there, I’m trying to clean up blocks that don’t work from the various builder matrix fields and get that into a workable product. Definitely lots of thread pulling. I tug on one, and another unravels somewhere...

Alt Text: I understand your where you’re going with this, and it does seem logical. However, it's important to consider that implementing this change will complicate the editing process for Aspen. Many of the staff members who update the site are not deeply involved in the process and often opt for the simplest solutions. I’m kind of "thinking out loud" as I write this, so if you’d like to talk this over on the phone, please feel free to call. I think the current method may encounter two primary challenges:

• Instead of staff being able to upload an image on the same page or entry that they’re editing, they’ll now have to plan ahead before editing and upload their image(s) first, then proceed to the entry afterward, which adds some extra steps and time to the process for them, and also removes a previously available function, which is rarely received well. On a one-off edit that’s not a huge deal, but if they’re publishing lots of content at once, that may add a significant amount of time and cause some frustration.
• As part of the process of uploading an asset directly to the library, I was never specifically prompted to enter ALT text. That means we’ll be relying on 20+ people to remember that after uploading the file, they need to enter the text as well by clicking on the image. I expect the success rate will be (far) less than stellar, even with multiple trainings and reminders.

On the plus side, I see how this method would keep the alt text centralized. If they use the file in multiple locations, we’re not cluttering the database with multiple text fields serving alt text to the same image if we were to specify that and the entry/page level instead of the asset level. The downside is the extra work and lack of requirement/prompt that the staff experience.

A few resulting questions:

1. Is there any way you’re aware of to require or prompt staff to enter alt text immediately after uploading a file directly within the asset library?
2. If me had to take the long route and build an alt text field into the affected entry types that have an image option, the same question applies: is there a way to require alt text only if an image is uploaded?

I may need to talk through this a bit more with my main contact at Aspen (Andy) and get his feedback. Programmatically, I understand it’s far easier on you and I do take the route you currently have implemented (and also cleaner programmatically), but I worry we’ll be making their jobs harder. That never goes over well and kind of mirrors some of the unilateral decisions Mark made that have caused lingering frustration on their end, so I’d like to avoid a repeat of that if at all possible.

Let me know what you think...

Shaun Cooney } MONUMENT GRAPHICS | DESIGN + WEB
PO Box 299, Fruita, CO 81521
p* 970/242-4311 • MonumentGraphics.com

*Alt Text*: I'm jumping back into this first today. If you mean the
walkthroughs in the video then just the "Adult Image" to test it in the
Sandbox for the last step. I added the field and "required" tag to all
images. I've updated all the relevant files with a "ternary operator" -
basically, if there is alt text specified, then use the alt text for the
alt attribute and if not, then use the title for the image.

As you mentioned previously, the title strips the filename of underscores,
dashes, etc. and the code now refers to this title as an alt text fallback.
The problem with this is the titles (and file names) are not always
descriptive of the image. Here's two examples:

[image: Screenshot 2024-04-08 at 10.08.36 AM.png]
There's also others like IMG 0157 & IMG 8109 that aren't descriptive.
[image: Screenshot 2024-04-08 at 10.04.46 AM.png]
This is the example in production and looks the same in development. So the
code appears to be working properly but can be helped by having descriptive
filenames.

The other side, ensuring the alt text is required on the fields (referenced
in your image), I think the simplest and best solution to this is to limit
the "Add a File" to not allow images to be uploaded through then implement
the solutions I've mentioned which will force Aspen to go through the "Add
an Image" - i.e Assets. Handling it this way should have the effect we're
seeking.

Let me know if this makes sense or if it needs further explanation. I'm
also available for a call today if that's easier.

Date: Fri, 5 Apr 2024 14:50:36 -0600

Subject: Re: Accordions

I like the looks of that plugin as a fallback in case we ever need it. Please proceed with installation.

AR-40: Empty hearing is definitely a CMS issue. I’ll clean that up. It’s easy with those WYSIWYG editors to have stray code like that. I’ll remind the staff, but the reality is that most people aren’t detailed oriented enough to notice if it does happen, so there are likely to be cases where this happens. If someone could actually sue Aspen for that minor of a mistake, then the whole law needs to be re-thought. All that to say, I’m not too worried about it...

AR-67: If there’s a way to make sure links formed via Redactor have text, I’m all for that. Otherwise, this is kind of like AR-40, above. A minor mistake caused by technology that shouldn’t affect overall accessibility of the site.

AR-68: The Scholarship pages contains both English and Spanish information. I’m not sure what to do in this case as the page isn’t a single language, so marking it as such seems misrepresentative. I’m content to let this one slide unless there’s a reasonably easy fix you’re aware of?

Alt Tags: In most cases, Mark seems to have included some fallback for the alt tags, but it changes from location to location. That’s not necessarily a bad thing. I’m not sure if he built this in, or if it’s a function of Craft, but in some locations, it seems to take the filename, strip out anything like dashes, then output the filename in a form of “clean” text. I think that’s a decent fallback, but I’m certainly open to other suggestions as well if you have better ideas. Of course the first order of business is to the get the alt field tied in when uploading and required, then make sure that field is being output on the front-end.

Right, the aria-label is used primarily to give meaning to tags that
otherwise wouldn't have that meaning to screen readers - like the X for a
close button. If Aspen is consistent with using anchor tags with meaningful
titles then the aria-label isn't necessary on anchor tags.

The plugin is just a visual reminder if you want to use it.

Hi Eric,

AR-64: The h4 is definitely coming from the CMS. However, I need to think through what will work best as an overall solution for headings. They’re definitely a mess and the ordering issues came up in my video review with BeAccessible back at the time of the audit. I think one aspect of creating a comprehensive solution will be to give Aspen more access to heading levels in the rich text editor. Mark was inconsistent about that. In most places, only H3 and H4 are available. In others, H2 and H5 are also offered. Since I think all pages generate H1 tags automatically, I’d like to make sure all rich text areas can utilize h2-h6 tags since that would give us some more flexibility to accommodate ordering issues that may come up in the code. As noted on the spreadsheet, the status update heading should definitely be changed so that it doesn’t utilize a heading tag. I’ll be in touch with more of an overall plan...

AR-65: There’s still a skipped heading from h2 —› h4. Hold off on any further changes for the moment. Looking through the site, they haven’t used the blog since 2021. I wonder if we could just eliminate that? From your end, is that an option?

In regard to the contact form, I’m really hesitant to pin the functionality of that marked fields section on any language that can be edited by the staff. Murphy’s law applies: if it can go wrong, it most likely will. I’d prefer to find a way to render that phrase without it depending on other text if at all possible. If needed, the asterisk isn’t required to be red that I know of, so it could all be one color if that simplifies it. (I’d mentioned that earlier as it makes it easier to identify, but I don’t think it’s a WCAG item).

Is there anything else you need input on for the time being?

Small note on the "Marked Fields" section above the contact us form: I was
able to create a dynamic render for that by stripping the HTML tags inside
the "Got a General Question or Comment?" title and matching the rendering
of the "Marked Fields" section to this exact phrase.

There's a downside to this method that if that phrase is ever changed in
the future then it will stop rendering the "Marked Fields" section. It's an
easy fix to just match the phrase again, but there also may be a more
elegant solution. Maybe something to come back to, but for now I'm going to
keep going on other issues.

> > > > > > > > > > Operating systems have a native indication of focus, which is available in many user agents. The default rendering of the focus indicator isn't always highly visible and may even be difficult to see against certain backgrounds. However, many platforms allow the user to customize the rendering of this focus indicator. Assistive technology can also change the appearance of the native focus indicator.

>>> Operating systems have a native indication of focus, which is available
>>>> in many user agents. The default rendering of the focus indicator isn't
>>>> always highly visible and may even be difficult to see against certain
>>>> backgrounds. However, many platforms allow the user to customize the
>>>> rendering of this focus indicator. Assistive technology can also change the
>>>> appearance of the native focus indicator.

On the twig error: sorry, that's my bad.  It's back up now. I found that
the "Fields marked" paragraph was showing in another section so I put an
"if" statement on it to only render with the contentForm, but I used a JS
operator instead of the Twig operator.

I've pushed the global focus for 2px solid white border and 2px solid blue
outline for all a, button, input, textarea and summary tags. One small
caveat to this approach is that the border will shift the  element slightly
when focused. We could simply use outline-offset, which will provide
distance from the element and won't shift but won't have contrast against
dark backgrounds.

This may need a little fine-tuning but I think this solution gets us most
of the way there on the focus indicator issues.

If you want to view or adjust the css it's all in one file at src > css >
global.pcss.

The modal was the bug I was working on when I switched to getting the list
done. I will be coming back to it asap.

Side note: the tab order on many pages started with the <div
id="page-container"> instead of the Nav. I put tabindex="-1" on the
page-container so that the first tab index is the Nav. I don't recall this
in the AR's but I saw it and it was a quick fix so I just took care of it -
hope that's alright.

Subject: Re: Accordions

Ok, I put a white border around submit on focus. On my computer, the focus
indicator looks different for different browsers - some not visibly
accessible. Perhaps this is a non-issue though -  I have been reading on
the focus indicator at w3.org <https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20-TECHS/G165.html>
and:

Operating systems have a native indication of focus, which is available in
> many user agents. The default rendering of the focus indicator isn't always
> highly visible and may even be difficult to see against certain
> backgrounds. However, many platforms allow the user to customize the
> rendering of this focus indicator. Assistive technology can also change the
> appearance of the native focus indicator.


It goes on to say that we have to change the focus settings at the global
level to override the browser defaults.

I just took care of AR-55 and AR-56 too. AR-55 I also put a 2px margin on
top and left to give room for the focus outline to show. AR-56 seemed to be
consistently the Title and Sign Up option in the first and second columns
so I named them as such. Those are both hardcoded.

As always, let me know if I need to adjust anything.

<br>
Regarding the focus trap, I’m sure you’ve consulted a lot of sources already. If it’s helpful and not overstepping, I had&nbsp;<a href="https://uxdesign.cc/how-to-trap-focus-inside-modal-to-make-it-ada-compliant-6a50f9a70700" target="_blank">this article</a>&nbsp;bookmarked for cases where I may need to implement this on other sites. I haven’t tested it, so maybe it’s garbage, but thought I’d share just in case.<br>
<br>
Concerning the focus indicator the more I’ve navigated around the site, the more I’ve realized that forcing a standard color in the code may prove problematic. As the focus shifts over white, green, blue, and orange backgrounds we may find we need to contextualize the styling. Please keep me updated on what you find as you begin working on that. I’d hate to see you spend too much time on it only to find we have to shift approaches, so let’s keep that one on a short leash for the time being.<br>
